description: We are a team passionate about space, science, and technology, with a strong interest in turning creative ideas into reality. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to develop innovative solutions using our problem-solving, and teamwork skills. We are interested in coding, game development, graphic design, animation, artificial intelligence, and data analysis. We welcome creative, responsible, and collaborative people who are excited to learn, and create something meaningful together.
summary:
AFTER IMPACT is a 3D educational survival game built in Godot. The player is an astronaut stranded at the Moon’s south pole after a crash landing, with no link to Earth and 90 days to survive. Every mission is based on NASA’s real research: extracting water and oxygen from lunar ice (LCROSS/LRO, ISRU), recycling water and air (ISS ECLSS), powering the base through the lunar night with a Kilopower reactor, living in an inflatable BEAM habitat, shielding it under a regolith dome, and growing food in a Veggie-style greenhouse. In the end, the player builds an antenna, sends a distress call to Earth and is rescued.

NASA’s plans for a habitable lunar base mostly stay in technical reports and scientific papers, out of reach for young people. AFTER IMPACT turns that knowledge into play. Each step shows why it matters, science cards cite real NASA sources, and every engineering decision has a consequence in the game. Students learn resource management, systems thinking and space science by doing, not just reading.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?
AFTER IMPACT is a 3D survival game. You play an astronaut who crash-lands at the Moon’s south pole with no contact with Earth and has to survive 90 days. The game has four phases, and each one is based on real NASA research:

  1. Survive the crash: check oxygen, power and damage.
  2. Mine lunar ice for water and oxygen, and build a Kilopower nuclear reactor for the lunar night.
  3. Build an inflatable habitat, solar arrays and a power grid.
  4. Protect the base with a regolith dome and a lava tube shelter, and grow food in a greenhouse.

Finally, the player builds an antenna, sends a distress message to Earth and is rescued. Every step shows what to do, where to go and why it matters. Science cards explain each system and link to NASA sources.

What benefits does it have?
It turns complex space science into something students can understand and experience. Players learn limited resource management, life support systems, energy balance, radiation protection and engineering decision-making in a hands-on way. It can be used at home or in classrooms, and it shows clearly which values come from real data and which are simplified for gameplay.

What is the intended impact of the project?
NASA’s plans for a habitable lunar base mostly stay in technical reports and scientific papers that young people never read. We want to bring that knowledge to middle school, high school and university students, spark their interest in space science and engineering, and help prepare the generation that may one day live and work on the Moon.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Game engine: Godot Engine 4.x
  • Programming language: GDScript
  • 3D content: All models, terrain and effects are generated procedurally in code. No external 3D assets were used.
  • Audio: Sound effects and music are generated procedurally in code.
  • Testing: An automated test suite of 253 checks that play through the whole game and verify every phase.
  • AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) for coding support and research.
  • Research sources: NASA reports, NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) and NASA mission pages.
  • Presentation and sharing: Canva and Google Drive.
  • Hardware: Standard Windows PCs.

How is your project creative?
Instead of reading about NASA’s research, the player lives it. Every mission is a real NASA concept (LCROSS ice discovery, ISS ECLSS, Kilopower, BEAM, Veggie) turned into gameplay with real choices, such as how thick the radiation shield should be or which light to use for plants. The story has an emotional arc: alone after a crash, building a home step by step, and finally being rescued while the camera rises over everything the player built. The game also labels what is real data and what is a game rule, so it teaches honestly.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific accuracy: We used real NASA data and labeled every simplified value.
  • Accessibility: We designed clear guidance so players never get lost: big orange mission banners, a guiding light beam, and “What, Why, Where” hints.
  • Target age: Content is understandable for middle school students but still useful for university students.
  • Engagement: Story, visuals, music and a cinematic ending keep players motivated.
  • Playtime: A chapter select menu lets players and teachers jump straight to any phase.
  • Reliability: Automated tests and bug fixes make sure the game can be completed from start to finish.
  • Low requirements: The game runs on ordinary computers without extra downloads or assets.
